specAnchors.text: know that magnetism is induced in some materials when they are placed in a magnetic field

primer.text: Permanent magnets keep their poles for decades; induced magnets borrow them for as long as the field lasts. This note sorts the magnetic family — iron, steel, cobalt, nickel — into hard keepers and soft losers, and shows why a magnet plus an unmagnetised material can only ever attract.

modules.title: Magnetic materials and the permanent/induced split
modules.opening: Only a short list of substances — iron, steel, cobalt, nickel — respond to magnets at all. Permanent magnets hold their magnetism indefinitely; induced magnets are ordinary magnetic materials that gain poles only while sitting in a field, and always pull towards whatever induced them.
keyPoints: Magnetic materials include iron, steel, cobalt, nickel and alloys containing them.
Non-magnetic materials such as copper, aluminium, plastic and glass are unaffected by magnetic fields.
A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field continuously.
An induced magnet is a magnetic material that becomes magnetised only while in another magnet's field.
The force between a magnet and an induced magnet is always attraction.

low.restatement: A fridge magnet works forever — it is permanent. A paperclip only sticks while it is near the magnet — it is an induced magnet, gaining and losing its pull with the field.
low.analogy: A permanent magnet is a lamp with its own battery; an induced magnet is a reflective panel that shines only while the lamp is on.
low.examPointer: Use the phrase 'while placed in the magnetic field' for induced magnetism — the timing condition is the mark.

medium.restatement: The distinction is persistence of domain alignment: permanent (hard) materials lock their aligned domains, sustaining a field with no external help; induced (soft) materials align only under the applied field and randomise when it leaves. Induction always yields attraction because the alignment places the unlike pole nearest the inducing pole.
medium.analogy: A permanent magnet is a marching band that keeps formation after the music stops; an induced magnet is the band that snaps into step only while the drum plays.
medium.examPointer: For the 'always attraction' claim, justify it geometrically: induced pole nearest the magnet is always unlike, and unlike poles attract.

modules.title: Permanent magnets at work, inducing and losing magnetism
modules.opening: Permanent magnets are engineered to forget nothing: hard steels keep their aligned domains for decades. Induced magnets do the opposite — poles appear the moment a field arrives, with the unlike pole always facing the source, and vanish the moment it leaves.
keyPoints: Permanent magnets are made from magnetically hard materials such as steel.
A permanent magnet keeps its field without any external magnet nearby.
Induced magnetism appears only while the material sits in the magnetic field.
The induced pole nearest the inducing magnet is always unlike that pole.
Removing the field — or the magnet — lets an induced magnet lose its magnetism.

low.restatement: A steel fridge magnet never switches off. An iron tack held near it grows a south pole on the side facing the magnet's north pole — and loses it again when taken away.
low.analogy: Permanent magnetism is a tattoo; induced magnetism is a stamp that fades as soon as the stamp is lifted.
low.examPointer: Name the induced pole explicitly in diagram questions: near a north pole, the near face becomes south.

medium.restatement: Induction is domain alignment under an external field: the nearest-face domains flip to present the unlike pole, minimising the system's field energy, which is why the resulting force is attraction. Hard materials resist realignment both ways — that is why they hold permanent magnetism but are slow to induce; soft materials flip freely in both directions.
medium.analogy: Soft material is a crowd that instantly faces whoever shouts; hard material is a crowd that turns slowly but then refuses to turn back.
medium.examPointer: Chain questions: each newly induced clip induces the next — say 'each clip acts as the inducing magnet for the next' for the evaluation mark.

glossary.definition: A magnet made of hard magnetic material that keeps its field without external help.
A substance, such as iron, steel, cobalt or nickel, that a magnet can attract or induce.
The lining-up of tiny magnetic regions inside a material that gives it net magnetism.

workedExample.prompt: The diagram shows a magnet held close to a piece of metal that is suspended by a light cotton thread. The piece of metal is attracted towards the magnet. Explain this observation, and state what it does and does not prove about the metal.
steps: The magnet's field acts on the suspended metal, so magnetism is induced in it while the field is present.
Induction always places an unlike induced pole nearest the magnet, so the force between them is attraction.
The observation proves the metal is a magnetic substance; it does not prove the metal was already a magnet, because either pole of the magnet would attract it.
A certain test would be to check for repulsion with the magnet's pole — only a true magnet can repel.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The metal is attracted because magnetism is induced in it by the magnet's field; this shows it is a magnetic material but does not show it was magnetised beforehand.
